rationale: SGA-to-FGA switch — cost-driven or for high D2 occupancy requirements beyond the SGA range. Both risperidone and haloperidol are potent D2 antagonists with significant EPS risk; the pharmacological step is smaller than from olanzapine or quetiapine. Prolactin remains high throughout (both agents are prolactin-raising). Key concern is the shift in QTc risk: risperidone has low QTc risk while haloperidol is high — baseline ECG before starting haloperidol. EPS burden may worsen at equivalent doses as haloperidol is the more EPS-prone agent. Anticholinergic co-prescription review: if the patient is already on benzhexol for risperidone-related EPS, continue it; if not, have a low threshold to start once haloperidol is dominant. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start haloperidol 2 mg. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Baseline ECG mandatory. Assess EPS carefully at each visit.
Increase haloperidol to 5 mg target. Plateau risperidone — allow haloperidol to stabilise before tapering.
Begin tapering risperidone to 3 mg. Monitor for EPS worsening as haloperidol becomes the dominant AP.
Reduce risperidone to 2 mg. Prescribe benzhexol if EPS emerging. Recheck QTc — haloperidol's QTc contribution now significant.
Reduce risperidone to 1 mg. Haloperidol providing primary antipsychotic cover.
Stop risperidone. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Document metabolic baseline — expect improvement. Consider depot (haloperidol decanoate) if adherence is a concern.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: risperidone 4 mg ≈ haloperidol 5 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
